description: Removing duplicates in Excel can delete valid records if you choose the wrong column. This quick example shows why names are not reliable unique keys and why you should review duplicates before deletion. #excel #data #tutorial #productivity

scenes.title: Don't deduplicate Excel by name.
scenes.narration: Excel's Remove Duplicates button is useful, but the wrong key can delete real records.

scenes.title: These rows are not duplicates.
scenes.narration: Look at these two rows. Both customers are named Alex Lee, but they have different email addresses and different customer IDs.

scenes.title: Name is a bad unique key.
body: Selecting only Name can merge real people
A convenient column is not automatically unique
scenes.note: Do not delete until the duplicate rule is verified.
scenes.narration: If you remove duplicates using only the Name column, one real customer can disappear.

scenes.title: Use the field that should be unique.
scenes.note: Confirm the key's uniqueness rule before deletion.
scenes.narration: Instead, decide what should actually be unique. For customer data, that might be a customer ID or another verified key.

scenes.title: Flag first. Delete second.
scenes.narration: Before deleting anything, flag the duplicates first and review the affected rows.

scenes.title: Trusted key > convenient column
scenes.narration: The rule is simple: deduplicate by a trusted key, not by a convenient-looking column. That keeps cleanup fast without silently throwing away valid data.
